meta.title: Lua Programming Language
meta.subtitle: From zero to a LuaRaylib game — the scripting language embedded in GnuchanOS.

sections.title: Why Lua?
paragraphs: Lua is a small, fast scripting language designed to be embedded inside a bigger program. That is exactly how GnuchanOS uses it: the GCL runtime starts a Lua interpreter in-process and hands it a raylib window, so a Lua script can open a window, draw and play sound without any build step.
The whole language fits in a few hundred kilobytes. There is no compile phase — you write a .lua file, run it, and it executes immediately.
This track has two halves. The first half teaches the language itself (Lua). The second half teaches LuaRaylib, the binding that exposes raylib and raygui to Lua.

notes.text: Everything in this track runs on the Lua that ships with GnuchanOS (Lua_Runtime/lua.dll) together with LuaRaylib.dll and LuaRaygui.dll.

sections.title: Your First Program
paragraphs: print writes a line to standard output. It is a function, not a statement, and it accepts any number of values.

code.src:
print("Hello from Lua!")
print("One line", "and another value")

sections.output:
Hello from Lua!
One line	and another value

sections.title: Comments
paragraphs: A line comment starts with two dashes. A block comment uses --[[ ... ]], and adding an extra dash (--[==[ ... ]==]) lets you nest comment markers inside it.

code.src:
-- a single line comment

--[[
   a block comment
   spanning several lines
]]

local x = 5  -- trailing comment
print(x)

sections.title: Three Ways to Run Lua
paragraphs: The runtime is always the same; only the entry point changes.
1. Standalone file. The GCL CLI can run a Lua file directly.
2. From GCL. The Embed module starts a Lua process and can share variables with it.
3. From the IDE. A project created with the Lua switch on already contains scripts/main.lua.

code.src:
# 1. run a file directly
gcl -luarun hello.lua

# 2. start Lua from a GCL program
#    (main.gcsf)
#    #native <Embed>
#    Embed.Run(type="lua");
#    Embed.Stop(type="lua");

# 3. build a project that opens a Lua window
gcl -build project.gcdata

notes.text: When Lua runs under GCL, three globals already exist before your first line: raylib, raygui and gcl. You never have to require them.

sections.title: The Eight Types
paragraphs: Lua is dynamically typed: a variable has no type, the value does. There are eight types, and type() tells you which one you are holding.

rows: A value you can pass around
C data owned by a library

sections.title: Global and Local Variables
paragraphs: A plain assignment creates a global variable. Adding local before the name creates a variable that dies at the end of the enclosing block — it is faster and it cannot leak into other files.
Prefer local almost everywhere. A typo in a global name silently creates a new global instead of failing, which is the classic Lua bug.

code.src:
total = 10          -- global
local count = 3     -- local

local a, b = 1, 2   -- multiple assignment
print(a, b)         -- 1   2

a, b = b, a         -- swap, no temporary needed
print(a, b)         -- 2   1

local name, age = "Emre"
print(name, age)    -- Emre   nil
print(type(name), type(age))

sections.title: Numbers
paragraphs: Numbers are integers or floats, and Lua converts between them when it needs to. Integer division is written //, raising to a power is ^, and there are no surprises with % on negatives.

code.src:
print(7 / 2)        -- 3.5   (float division)
print(7 // 2)       -- 3     (integer division)
print(7 % 2)        -- 1
print(-7 % 3)       -- 2     (result takes the sign of the divisor)
print(2 ^ 10)       -- 1024.0
print(10 / 2)       -- 5.0
print(3 == 3.0)     -- true
print(math.type(3), math.type(3.0))

sections.title: Strings and Concatenation
paragraphs: The .. operator concatenates strings, and # returns their length. Numbers are converted automatically when concatenated, but code is clearer when you convert explicitly with tostring.

code.src:
local first = "Gnuchan"
local last = "OS"
local full = first .. " " .. last

print(full)                 -- Gnuchan OS
print(#full)                -- 10
print("pi = " .. 3.14159)   -- number -> string automatically
print(tostring(42), tonumber("42"))
print(tonumber("0x1F"))     -- 31
print(tonumber("abc"))      -- nil  (not a number)

sections.title: Arithmetic, Concatenation and Length
paragraphs: Lua has the arithmetic operators you expect plus // (floor division), ^ (power), .. (concatenation) and # (length).

code.src:
local a, b = 17, 5
print(a + b, a - b, a * b)   -- 22  12  85
print(a / b)                 -- 3.4
print(a // b, a % b)         -- 3   2
print(a ^ 2)                 -- 289.0
print(-a)                    -- -17

print("Gnuchan" .. "OS")       -- GnuchanOS
print(#"GnuchanOS")            -- 9
print(#{ 10, 20, 30 })         -- 3

sections.title: Comparison and Equality
paragraphs: The relational operators are == ~= < > <= >=. Note that not equal is ~=, not !=.

Comparison operators never mix types: comparing a number with a string raises an error instead of silently converting. Equality (==) never errors — two different types are simply not equal. Tables and functions are compared by reference, so two tables with the same contents are still different values.

code.src:
print(10 == 10, 10 ~= 10)   -- true   false
print(2 < 3, 3 <= 3)       -- true   true
print(1 == "1")            -- false (different types, no error)

local t1 = { 1, 2 }
local t2 = { 1, 2 }
local t3 = t1
print(t1 == t2)            -- false (two different tables)
print(t1 == t3)            -- true  (same table)

sections.output:
true	false
true	true
false
false
true

sections.title: and, or, not — and the Truthiness Rule
paragraphs: Exactly two values are false in Lua: false and nil. Everything else is true — including 0 and the empty string "". This differs from C and Python and is a common source of confusion.
and and or short-circuit and return one of their operands, not a boolean. That is what makes the two idioms below work.

code.src:
print(0 and "zero is true")     -- 0 is true in Lua
print("" and "empty is true")   -- "" is true too
print(nil and "never")          -- nil
print(false or "default")       -- default

-- default-value idiom (only when x is nil/false)
local x
local value = x or 100
print(value)                    -- 100

-- guard idiom: call only if the object exists
local obj
print(obj and obj.run)          -- nil, no error

sections.output:
zero is true
empty is true
nil
default
100
nil

sections.title: Precedence
paragraphs: From highest to lowest: ^, then unary not # - ~, then * / // %, then + -, then .., then == ~= < > <= >=, then and, then or. When in doubt, parenthesise — concatenation next to arithmetic is the usual trap.

code.src:
print(2 + 3 * 4)          -- 14
print(-2 ^ 2)             -- -4.0  (^ binds tighter than unary -)
print((-2) ^ 2)           -- 4.0
print(1 < 2 and 2 < 3)    -- true
print(1 .. 2 + 3)         -- 15  (arithmetic first, then concat)
print("a" .. "b" .. "c")   -- abc

sections.title: if / elseif / else
paragraphs: Conditions need no parentheses. Every block is closed with end, and the word is elseif — one word.

code.src:
local score = 85

if score >= 90 then
    print("AA")
elseif score >= 80 then
    print("BA")
elseif score >= 70 then
    print("BB")
else
    print("retry")
end

sections.title: while and repeat
paragraphs: while tests before the body. repeat ... until tests after it, so the body always runs at least once. The condition in until can see the locals declared inside the body.

code.src:
local count = 3
while count > 0 do
    print("count = " .. count)
    count = count - 1
end

local n = 0
repeat
    n = n + 1
until n >= 3
print("n = " .. n)

sections.title: Numeric for
paragraphs: The numeric loop takes start, stop and an optional step. All three are evaluated once, before the loop starts.

code.src:
for i = 1, 5 do
    io.write(i, " ")
end
print()

for i = 10, 1, -2 do
    io.write(i, " ")
end
print()

-- the loop variable is local to the loop
local i = "outside"
for i = 1, 2 do end
print(i)

sections.title: Generic for: pairs and ipairs
paragraphs: ipairs walks the array part from index 1 and stops at the first nil. pairs walks every key, in an order Lua does not promise — never rely on it for output.
In this book the key/value form is written for k, v in pairs(t). Inside the loop the pair comes back in the order key, value.

code.src:
local fruits = { "apple", "pear", "plum" }
for index, name in ipairs(fruits) do
    print(index, name)
end

local player = { name = "Emre", score = 120 }
for key, value in pairs(player) do
    print(key, value)
end

sections.output:
1	apple
2	pear
3	plum
name	Emre
score	120

sections.title: break and goto
paragraphs: break leaves the innermost loop. Lua also has goto with labels, which is the clean way to jump out of a nested loop.

code.src:
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i == 4 then break end
    io.write(i, " ")
end
print()

for i = 1, 3 do
    for j = 1, 3 do
        if i * j == 6 then goto done end
    end
end
::done::
print("escaped both loops")

sections.title: Defining and Calling
paragraphs: A function is a value created with function ... end and stored in a variable. Parameters need no types and no parentheses around the call are required for a single string argument.

code.src:
local function add(a, b)
    return a + b
end

print(add(3, 4))          -- 7
print(add(1.5, 2.5))      -- 4.0

local function greet(name)
    return "Hello " .. (name or "stranger")
end
print(greet("Emre"))
print(greet())

sections.title: Multiple Return Values
paragraphs: A function may return several values, and a caller may take as many as it wants. This is how the raylib binding hands back an image: the data pointer, the width and the height in one call.
When a call is not the last item in a list, only its first result is kept.

code.src:
local function minmax(a, b)
    if a < b then return a, b else return b, a end
end

local lo, hi = minmax(9, 3)
print(lo, hi)             -- 3   9

local function three() return 1, 2, 3 end
print(three())            -- 1   2   3
print(three(), "extra")   -- 1   extra  (only the first survives)

sections.title: Varargs
paragraphs: Three dots collect any number of arguments. select("#", ...) returns how many were passed, and select(n, ...) returns them starting from position n.

code.src:
local function count(...)
    return select("#", ...)
end

local function sum(...)
    local total = 0
    for _, v in ipairs({ ... }) do total = total + v end
    return total
end

print(count(1, 2, 3))     -- 3
print(sum(10, 20, 32))    -- 62
print(select(2, "a", "b", "c"))

sections.title: Closures
paragraphs: A function remembers the locals of the scope it was created in. That combination — function plus captured variables — is a closure, and it is how Lua builds counters, iterators and modules without any special syntax.

code.src:
local function counter()
    local n = 0
    return function()
        n = n + 1
        return n
    end
end

local next1 = counter()
local next2 = counter()
print(next1(), next1(), next1())  -- 1   2   3
print(next2())                    -- 1  (its own n)

sections.title: Recursion
paragraphs: A recursive function that calls itself by name must be declared as local function (which introduces the name before the body) or the recursive name will be nil inside the body.

code.src:
local function fact(n)
    if n <= 1 then return 1 end
    return n * fact(n - 1)
end

print(fact(5))   -- 120
print(fact(10))  -- 3628800

sections.title: One Structure To Rule Them All
paragraphs: Lua has no arrays, no lists, no dictionaries and no structs. It has tables, and every one of those is a table used in a particular way: a list is a table with integer keys from 1, a dictionary is a table with string keys, an object is a table with functions in it.
A table is created with braces. Keys are written either key = value or inside square brackets, and the value of a key that was never assigned is nil.

code.src:
-- list (array): integer keys start at 1
local fruits = { "apple", "pear", "plum" }
print(fruits[1], fruits[2], fruits[3])   -- apple  pear  plum
print(#fruits)                            -- 3

-- dictionary: string keys
local player = { name = "Emre", score = 120 }
print(player.name, player["score"])       -- Emre  120
print(player.missing)                     -- nil

-- mixed and nested
local grid = {
    [1] = { 1, 0, 0 },
    [2] = { 0, 1, 0 },
    title = "matrix"
}
print(grid[2][2], grid.title)             -- 1   matrix

sections.output:
apple	pear	plum
3
Emre	120
nil
1	matrix

sections.title: Adding and Removing
paragraphs: The table library is the standard toolkit: insert, remove, concat, sort and unpack.
#t is only well defined when the table has no holes — no nil in the middle of the list part.

code.src:
local list = { "b", "a", "c" }

table.insert(list, "d")          -- append at the end
table.insert(list, 1, "z")       -- insert at position 1
print(table.concat(list, ", "))  -- z, b, a, c, d

local removed = table.remove(list, 1)   -- remove position 1
print(removed, #list)                   -- z   4

table.sort(list)
print(table.concat(list, ", "))         -- a, b, c, d

local x, y, z = table.unpack({ 10, 20, 30 })
print(x, y, z)                          -- 10  20  30

sections.output:
z, b, a, c, d
z	4
a, b, c, d
10	20	30

sections.title: Iterating and 2D Tables
paragraphs: Numeric for walks a list, ipairs walks it and stops at the first hole, and pairs walks every key. Two nested loops walk a grid.

code.src:
local scores = { 12, 45, 7 }

local total = 0
for i = 1, #scores do
    total = total + scores[i]
end
print("total = " .. total)

local board = {
    { 1, 2, 3 },
    { 4, 5, 6 }
}
for row = 1, #board do
    local line = ""
    for col = 1, #board[row] do
        line = line .. board[row][col] .. " "
    end
    print(line)
end

sections.title: Tables Are References
paragraphs: Assigning a table copies the reference, not the contents. Two names pointing at the same table see each other's changes. To copy, build a new table and copy the fields — or use table.move for the list part.

code.src:
local original = { 1, 2, 3 }
local alias = original          -- same table!
alias[1] = 99
print(original[1])              -- 99

-- a real (shallow) copy
local copy = {}
for i = 1, #original do copy[i] = original[i] end
copy[1] = 1
print(original[1], copy[1])     -- 99   1

-- table.move(source, from, to, target)
local moved = {}
table.move({ "a", "b" }, 1, 2, 1, moved)
print(moved[1], moved[2])       -- a   b

sections.title: The string Library
paragraphs: Strings are immutable, so every string function returns a new string. Both string.sub(s, i) and the method form s:sub(i) work — the colon form is shorter and is what you will see in real code.
Indexes are 1-based, and negative indexes count from the end.

code.src:
local s = "GnuchanOS"

print(s:len())              -- 9
print(s:sub(1, 6))          -- Gnucha
print(s:sub(-2))            -- OS    (last two)
print(s:upper(), s:lower()) -- GNUCHANOS  gnuchanos
print(s:rep(2))             -- GnuchanOSGnuchanOS
print(s:reverse())          -- SOnaHCunG
print(string.byte("A"))      -- 65
print(string.char(71, 67))  -- GC
print(string.format("%s v%.2f", "GCL", 0.1))   -- GCL v0.10

sections.output:
9
Gnucha
OS
GNUCHANOS	gnuchanos
GnuchanOSGnuchanOS
SOnaHCunG
65
GC
GCL v0.10

sections.title: find, match and gmatch
paragraphs: find returns the start and end position of a match, match returns the captured text, and gmatch is an iterator over every match.

Lua has its own pattern language. It is much smaller than a regular expression engine: %a letters, %d digits, %s spaces, %w alphanumerics, . any character, * zero or more, + one or more, - the lazy version of *, and parentheses for captures. A literal magic character is escaped with %, so a literal dot is %..

code.src:
local csv = "apple,pear,plum"

print(csv:find("pear"))         -- 7   10
print(csv:match("(%a+),pear"))  -- apple

local text = "x=10, y=20, z=30"
for key, value in text:gmatch("(%a+)=(%d+)") do
    print(key, value)
end

-- extract all numbers
for n in ("a1 b22 c333"):gmatch("%d+") do
    io.write(n, " ")
end
print()

sections.title: gsub — Search and Replace
paragraphs: gsub replaces every match. The replacement may be a string (with %1, %2 for captures), a table keyed by the match, or a function that decides the replacement. It returns the new string and how many substitutions were made.

code.src:
local path = "assets/icon.png"

-- rename the extension
local png = path:gsub("%.png$", ".jpg")
print(png)                       -- assets/icon.jpg

-- capture groups
local date = "2026-09-16"
local d, m, y = date:match("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)")
print(y, m, d)                   -- 2026   09   16

-- function replacement: square every number
local squared = ("1 2 3"):gsub("%d+", function(n)
    return tonumber(n) ^ 2
end)
print(squared)                   -- 1 4 9

-- count
local _, count = ("a-b-c"):gsub("-", "_")
print("replacements: " .. count)  -- 2

sections.title: Long Strings and Escapes
paragraphs: Double and single quoted strings interpret escapes: \n, \t, \\, \" and \x41. A long string inside double square brackets interprets nothing — no escapes, no quotes to escape — which makes it ideal for embedding text, shader source or a whole file.

code.src:
local escaped = "line 1\nline 2\ttabbed"
print(escaped)

local raw = [[
    shader = {
        "vertex" : "...",
        "fragment" : "..."
    }
]]
print(raw)

-- a leading newline is skipped with [[ ... ]] ,
-- so the first printed line is the text itself.

sections.title: math
paragraphs: The math library is always available. Note that math.random() is not seeded automatically with a changing value, so seed it yourself when you want a different run every launch.

rows: Round down / up to an integer
x as an integer, or nil

code.src:
print(math.floor(3.7), math.ceil(3.2))   -- 3   4
print(math.max(3, 9, 4), math.min(3, 9, 4)) -- 9   3
print(math.sqrt(81), 2 ^ 0.5)              -- 9.0   1.4142135623731
print(math.floor(math.pi * 100) / 100)     -- 3.14

math.randomseed(os.time())
print(math.random(1, 6))   -- a die roll

sections.title: os
paragraphs: os.time() returns the current Unix time and is also the usual seed for the random generator. os.clock() measures elapsed CPU time, useful for timing a piece of code.

code.src:
print(os.date("%Y-%m-%d"))
print(type(os.time()))

local start = os.clock()
local total = 0
for i = 1, 200000 do total = total + i end
print("sum = " .. total)
print("cpu seconds: " .. string.format("%.3f", os.clock() - start))

sections.title: io — Writing and Reading Files
paragraphs: io.write is like print without a newline and without tabs. io.open(path, mode) returns a file handle or nil plus an error message, so always check it.
Modes: "r" read, "w" write (truncate), "a" append, "rb" / "wb" binary.

code.src:
local path = "scores.txt"

-- write
local out = assert(io.open(path, "w"))
out:write("Emre 120\n")
out:write("Ada 150\n")
out:close()

-- append
local app = assert(io.open(path, "a"))
app:write("Linus 90\n")
app:close()

-- read every line
local f = assert(io.open(path, "r"))
for line in f:lines() do
    local name, score = line:match("(%a+) (%d+)")
    print(name, score)
end
f:close()

sections.title: Errors and pcall
paragraphs: error(msg) stops the program, assert(value, msg) only raises when the value is false or nil, and pcall(f, ...) calls a function in protected mode: it returns true plus the results on success, or false plus the error on failure. That is how a failing file open becomes a value you can inspect instead of a crash.
xpcall(f, handler) adds a message handler that runs before the stack unwinds — the hook a logger would use.

code.src:
local function divide(a, b)
    if b == 0 then error("division by zero") end
    return a / b
end

print(divide(10, 2))              -- 5.0

local ok, result = pcall(divide, 10, 0)
print(ok, result)                  -- false  .../errors.lua:2: division by zero

-- assert turns nil into an error
local f = io.open("missing.txt", "r")
print(f)                           -- nil
local ok2, err = pcall(assert, f, "file not found")
print(ok2, err)

-- xpcall with a handler
local ok3, msg = xpcall(function() error("boom") end, function(e)
    return "handled: " .. e
end)
print(ok3, msg)

sections.output:
5.0
false	errors.lua:2: division by zero
nil	nil
false	file not found
false	handled: errors.lua:16: boom

sections.title: A Module Is Just a Table
paragraphs: Lua has no package keyword. A module is an ordinary file that returns a table, and require("name") looks for name.lua on package.path, runs it once, and caches the returned value.
Because the result is cached, a second require of the same module returns the same table — which is also how a module can hold shared state.

code.src:
-- a module: collect the functions in a table and return it
local M = {}

M.pi = 3.14159265358979

function M.area(r)
    return M.pi * r * r
end

function M.clamp(value, lo, hi)
    if value < lo then return lo end
    if value > hi then return hi end
    return value
end

return M

notes.text: Keep everything inside the module local except the table you return. Nothing else leaks into the caller's globals.

sections.title: Using the Module
paragraphs: require resolves the name against package.path. To load from a sub-folder, either add that folder to the path or require the name with dots replaced by slashes, depending on the pattern in your path.

code.src:
local mymath = require("mymath")

print(mymath.pi)                  -- 3.14159265358979
print(mymath.area(2))             -- 12.566370614359
print(mymath.clamp(15, 0, 10))    -- 10

-- the module is cached: the same table comes back
print(require("mymath") == mymath) -- true

-- see where Lua looks for files
print(package.path)

sections.title: Module State
paragraphs: Anything stored in the module table lives for as long as the program runs. That is the standard way to keep a score board, a cache or a settings table in one place.

notes.text: This is exactly the pattern the raylib Lua bindings use: raylib and raygui are tables of C functions registered by luaopen_LuaRaylib and luaopen_LuaRaygui.

sections.title: What a Metatable Is
paragraphs: A metatable is a normal table attached to another value, and it changes how that value behaves. It is how Lua lets a table respond to +, to tostring, to being called like a function, and — most importantly — to a missing field lookup.

This is not an advanced footnote: it is how the raylib Lua binding works. raylib.Rectangle(10, 10, 200, 80) returns a userdata that carries a metatable, and that metatable is what makes rect.x return a number.

code.src:
local light = { x = 0, y = 0 }
local meta = {}   -- the metatable (currently empty)

setmetatable(light, meta)
print(getmetatable(light) == meta)   -- true
print(light.name)                    -- nil, no __index yet

sections.title: __index — Reading Missing Fields
paragraphs: When you read a key that is nil, Lua asks the metatable for __index. If it is a table, the lookup continues in that table. If it is a function, Lua calls it with the original table and the key, and uses whatever it returns.

sections.title: Operator Metamethods
paragraphs: Each operator has a metamethod name: __add, __sub, __mul, __div, __mod, __pow, __unm (unary minus), __concat, __len, __eq, __lt, __le, __call, __tostring, __newindex and __pairs.

code.src:
local Vector = {}
Vector.__index = Vector

function Vector.new(x, y)
    return setmetatable({ x = x, y = y }, Vector)
end

function Vector.__add(a, b)      return Vector.new(a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y) end
function Vector.__sub(a, b)      return Vector.new(a.x - b.x, a.y - b.y) end
function Vector.__eq(a, b)       return a.x == b.x and a.y == b.y end
function Vector.__tostring(v)    return "(" .. v.x .. ", " .. v.y .. ")" end
function Vector:length()         return math.sqrt(self.x ^ 2 + self.y ^ 2) end

local a = Vector.new(3, 4)
local b = Vector.new(1, 1)

print(a + b)          -- (4, 5)
print(a - b)          -- (2, 3)
print(a == Vector.new(3, 4))   -- true
print(a:length())     -- 5.0

sections.title: Objects and Inheritance
paragraphs: Two lines give you a class: Class.__index = Class makes instances find their methods, and calling the constructor with setmetatable tags the new table as an instance.
Inheritance is the same trick one level up: the child sets its own __index to the parent, so a missing method walks up the chain.

code.src:
local Animal = {}
Animal.__index = Animal

function Animal.new(name)
    return setmetatable({ name = name, legs = 4 }, Animal)
end

function Animal:speak()
    return self.name .. " makes a sound"
end

local Dog = setmetatable({}, { __index = Animal })   -- inherit
Dog.__index = Dog                                     -- instances use Dog

function Dog.new(name, breed)                        -- override
    local self = Animal.new(name)
    self.breed = breed
    return setmetatable(self, Dog)
end

function Dog:speak()                                 -- override
    return self.name .. " barks"
end

local animal = Animal.new("Cat")
local dog = Dog.new("Rex", "Kangal")

print(animal:speak())     -- Cat makes a sound
print(dog:speak())        -- Rex barks
print(dog.legs)           -- 4   (inherited field)
print(dog.name, dog.breed)

sections.output:
Cat makes a sound
Rex barks
4
Rex	Kangal

sections.title: __newindex and __call
paragraphs: __newindex runs when you assign to a key that does not exist yet, which lets an object validate or redirect writes. __call makes a table callable, so t(...) becomes t.__call(t, ...).

code.src:
local guarded = setmetatable({}, {
    __newindex = function(t, key, value)
        rawset(t, key, math.max(0, value))   -- never store a negative
    end
})
guarded.score = -50
print(guarded.score)      -- 0

local counter = setmetatable({ n = 0 }, {
    __call = function(self, step)
        self.n = self.n + (step or 1)
        return self.n
    end
})
print(counter())          -- 1
print(counter(10))        -- 11

sections.title: Three Functions
paragraphs: When Lua runs under GCL there is one extra global: gcl. It is a table with exactly three members, and it is the whole bridge between the two languages.

rows: Connect to the shared state block

notes.text: Shared values are numbers. Text travels as separate values, or by convention: store a length and a code, not a string.

sections.title: How the State Is Shared
paragraphs: The state block is shared memory that the GCL side also reaches through Embed.SendValue and Embed.GetValue. Both sides read and write the same named slots, so a Lua script and a GCL program can exchange values without opening a socket or a file.
Always call gcl.init() before the first get_state or set_state.

sections.title: The Lua Side
paragraphs: The Lua file reads with gcl.get_state and writes with gcl.set_state. Names must match on both sides — they are plain strings, so a typo reads nil rather than raising an error.
get_state returns a number, so guard against nil with the or idiom when a slot may not have been written yet.

code.src:
gcl.init()

local target = gcl.get_state("target_x") or 0.0
local speed  = gcl.get_state("speed") or 1.0

local x = 0.0
local score = 0

while x < target do
    x = x + speed
    score = score + 1
end

-- publish the result for the GCL side
gcl.set_state("score", score)
print("reached " .. x .. " in " .. score .. " steps")

sections.title: Two Processes, Two Windows
paragraphs: GCL can run Lua and Python at the same time — each is one process with its own window, and they talk through the same shared values. That is exactly how the Pong example in the GCL track works: Lua owns the left half of the world, Python owns the right half, and only the ball state is shared.

notes.text: Only one process per type: Embed.Run(type="lua") twice starts nothing the second time. Lua plus Python together is fine.

sections.title: What LuaRaylib Is
paragraphs: LuaRaylib is a C module that registers raylib's functions into a global Lua table called raylib. It is loaded automatically for you: when GCL starts a Lua script it calls luaopen_LuaRaylib and luaopen_LuaRaygui first, so raylib and raygui already exist when your script starts.
The binding exposes 209 raylib functions plus the raylib color and key constants, and 55 raygui functions.

sections.title: The Game Loop
paragraphs: Every raylib program has the same shape: open a window, loop until the user closes it, draw one frame per iteration, then close. In Lua the loop is an ordinary while loop and the condition is the return value of WindowShouldClose.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(800, 600, "My First LuaRaylib Window")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(50, 50, 200, 100, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawText("Hello from Lua + raylib", 20, 20, 30, raylib.BLACK)
    raylib.DrawFPS(10, 10)

    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Everything after InitWindow belongs inside the loop except CloseWindow. Drawing outside BeginDrawing / EndDrawing has no effect.

sections.title: Colors and Key Constants
paragraphs: Colors are integers, not tables. Every raylib color is a member of the raylib table: raylib.RED, raylib.DARKPURPLE, raylib.BLANK and so on. Keyboard and mouse constants have the same shape: raylib.KEY_SPACE, raylib.KEY_LEFT, raylib.MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT.
Functions that take a color simply take that integer.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Colors")

local colors = {
    raylib.RAYWHITE, raylib.RED, raylib.GREEN,
    raylib.BLUE, raylib.YELLOW, raylib.DARKPURPLE
}

print("first color value: " .. colors[1])
print("key space: " .. raylib.KEY_SPACE)

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Shapes
paragraphs: Every shape function takes plain numbers and an integer color. Coordinates are in pixels with the origin at the top-left of the window, y growing downwards.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(640, 360, "Shapes")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.BLACK)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(30, 30, 120, 60, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawRectangleLines(30, 110, 120, 60, raylib.GREEN)
    raylib.DrawCircle(280, 90, 40, raylib.BLUE)
    raylib.DrawCircleLines(400, 90, 40, raylib.YELLOW)
    raylib.DrawLine(30, 250, 600, 250, raylib.WHITE)
    raylib.DrawPoly(200, 250, 6, 40, 15, raylib.PURPLE)

    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Text
paragraphs: DrawText takes the text, then x, y, font size and color. MeasureText returns the width in pixels, which is what you need to centre or right-align a string.
TextFormat is Lua's version of string.format inside the binding; DrawFPS prints the frame rate.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(640, 240, "Text")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

local title = "LuaRaylib"
local score = 1234

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    local w = raylib.MeasureText(title, 40)
    raylib.DrawText(title, (640 - w) / 2, 40, 40, raylib.DARKPURPLE)

    local line = raylib.TextFormat("score: %i", score)
    raylib.DrawText(line, 20, 120, 24, raylib.MAROON)

    raylib.DrawFPS(500, 200)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: TextFormat / DrawText accept Lua strings directly — no buffer to declare, unlike the GCL binding.

sections.title: Rectangles as Values
paragraphs: raylib.Rectangle(x, y, w, h) returns a value you can store, pass around and read the fields of. It is a userdata with a metatable, so rect.x, rect.w and the rest read like ordinary table fields — and they can be assigned too.
This is the value raygui widgets expect, so it pays to build your layout once and reuse it.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Rectangle")

local box = raylib.Rectangle(50, 50, 200, 80)

print(box.x, box.y, box.w, box.h)   -- 50.0  50.0  200.0  80.0

box.w = 260                          -- fields are writable
print(box.w)                         -- 260.0

raylib.BeginDrawing()
raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)
raylib.DrawRectangleRec(box, raylib.SKYBLUE)
raylib.DrawRectangleLinesEx(box, 2, raylib.BLACK)
raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Textures
paragraphs: LoadTexture(path) returns a texture handle — an integer, not a table. Keep it in a variable, draw with it, and free it with UnloadTexture when the program ends, otherwise the GPU memory is released only at exit.
Images (LoadImage) return three values — data, width and height — and are usually loaded once to build a texture or a font.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(400, 300, "Texture")

local tex = raylib.LoadTexture("assets/icon.png")
print(raylib.IsTextureValid(tex))   -- boolean

raylib.BeginDrawing()
raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)
raylib.DrawTexture(tex, 100, 100, raylib.WHITE)
raylib.DrawTextureEx(tex, { x = 100, y = 100 }, 0.0, 2.0, raylib.WHITE)
raylib.EndDrawing()

raylib.UnloadTexture(tex)
raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Asset paths are resolved relative to the running script (or the project's raylib_asset_directory_path). If a texture fails to load its handle is not valid — check with IsTextureValid instead of drawing garbage.

sections.title: Keyboard
paragraphs: IsKeyDown(key) is true every frame the key is held — use it for movement. IsKeyPressed(key) is true only on the frame it went down — use it for a single action such as shooting or opening a menu.
Key codes are members of raylib: KEY_LEFT, KEY_RIGHT, KEY_UP, KEY_DOWN, KEY_W, KEY_A, KEY_S, KEY_D, KEY_SPACE, KEY_ESCAPE.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(640, 480, "Keyboard")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

local x, y = 320, 240
local SPEED = 200          -- pixels per second

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    -- GetFrameTime() is the seconds elapsed since the last frame,
    -- so multiplying by it makes movement frame-rate independent.
    local dt = raylib.GetFrameTime()

    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_LEFT)  then x = x - SPEED * dt end
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_RIGHT) then x = x + SPEED * dt end
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_UP)    then y = y - SPEED * dt end
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_DOWN)  then y = y + SPEED * dt end

    if raylib.IsKeyPressed(raylib.KEY_SPACE) then
        x, y = 320, 240        -- recentre, once per press
    end

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.DrawCircle(math.floor(x), math.floor(y), 20, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.DrawText("arrows to move, space to recentre", 10, 10, 20, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: GetFrameTime() returns a float — multiply every speed by it and the game plays the same at 30, 60 or 144 FPS.

sections.title: Mouse
paragraphs: GetMouseX() and GetMouseY() are integer screen coordinates. Buttons are tested with IsMouseButtonDown, IsMouseButtonPressed, IsMouseButtonReleased and IsMouseButtonUp using MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT, MOUSE_BUTTON_RIGHT or MOUSE_BUTTON_MIDDLE.
GetMouseWheelMove() returns the wheel delta for the current frame, and GetMouseDelta() returns how far the mouse moved since the last frame — the usual input for a free camera.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(640, 480, "Mouse")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    local mx = raylib.GetMouseX()
    local my = raylib.GetMouseY()

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    -- draw the cursor ring; click to fill it
    if raylib.IsMouseButtonDown(raylib.MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) then
        raylib.DrawCircle(mx, my, 18, raylib.ORANGE)
    end
    raylib.DrawCircleLines(mx, my, 24, raylib.DARKGRAY)

    if raylib.IsMouseButtonPressed(raylib.MOUSE_BUTTON_RIGHT) then
        print("right click at " .. mx .. ", " .. my)
    end

    raylib.DrawText("mouse: " .. mx .. ", " .. my, 10, 10, 20, raylib.BLACK)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Everything Else
paragraphs: Gamepads, touch and gestures follow the same shape: a predicate that returns a boolean and a constant that names the button.

rows: Change the key that closes the window

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Gamepad")

if raylib.IsGamepadAvailable(0) then
    print("gamepad 0: " .. raylib.GetGamepadName(0))
    local axis = raylib.GetGamepadAxisMovement(0, 0)
    print("left stick x: " .. string.format("%.2f", axis))
else
    print("no gamepad detected")
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Camera2D — Scrolling and Zooming
paragraphs: raylib.Camera2D() returns a table with four fields: offset (a table with x and y — where the camera's centre sits on the screen), target (the world point it looks at), rotation and zoom.
BeginMode2D(camera) switches drawing into world coordinates until EndMode2D(). Passing the camera table is what keeps the fields in Lua; you could also pass the six numbers in order.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(800, 600, "Camera2D")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

local camera = raylib.Camera2D()
camera.offset = { x = 400.0, y = 300.0 }   -- centre of the window
camera.target = { x = 0.0, y = 0.0 }       -- world point to look at
camera.zoom = 1.0

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    -- pan with WASD
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_D) then camera.target.x = camera.target.x + 4 end
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_A) then camera.target.x = camera.target.x - 4 end
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_W) then camera.target.y = camera.target.y - 4 end
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_S) then camera.target.y = camera.target.y + 4 end

    -- zoom with the wheel
    local wheel = raylib.GetMouseWheelMove()
    if wheel ~= 0 then
        camera.zoom = camera.zoom + wheel * 0.1
        if camera.zoom < 0.2 then camera.zoom = 0.2 end
    end

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.BLACK)

    raylib.BeginMode2D(camera)
        -- world space: this grid scrolls with the camera
        for x = -1000, 1000, 100 do
            raylib.DrawLine(x, -1000, x, 1000, raylib.DARKGRAY)
        end
        for y = -1000, 1000, 100 do
            raylib.DrawLine(-1000, y, 1000, y, raylib.DARKGRAY)
        end
        raylib.DrawCircle(0, 0, 30, raylib.RED)
    raylib.EndMode2D()

    -- screen space: this text never moves
    raylib.DrawText("WASD pan, wheel zoom", 10, 10, 20, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Indenting the block between BeginMode2D and EndMode2D is optional but makes it obvious which space a Draw* call lives in.

sections.title: Camera3D — A 3D View
paragraphs: raylib.Camera3D() returns a table with position, target and up (each a table with x, y, z), plus fovy and projection — the last one being raylib.CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE by default.
The classic starting camera sits at (10, 10, 10) looking at the origin. DrawGrid(slices, spacing) gives you a floor in one call.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(800, 600, "Camera3D")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

local camera = raylib.Camera3D()
camera.position = { x = 10.0, y = 10.0, z = 10.0 }
camera.target   = { x = 0.0,  y = 0.0,  z = 0.0 }
camera.up       = { x = 0.0,  y = 1.0,  z = 0.0 }
camera.fovy     = 45.0

local angle = 0.0

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    -- orbit the camera around the origin
    angle = angle + raylib.GetFrameTime() * 0.5
    camera.position.x = math.cos(angle) * 12
    camera.position.z = math.sin(angle) * 12

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    raylib.BeginMode3D(camera)
        raylib.DrawCube({ x = 0.0, y = 0.0, z = 0.0 }, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, raylib.RED)
        raylib.DrawCubeWires({ x = 0.0, y = 0.0, z = 0.0 }, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, raylib.MAROON)
        raylib.DrawGrid(10, 1.0)
    raylib.EndMode3D()

    raylib.DrawFPS(10, 10)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: The project template's 3D scene is exactly this shape — a Camera3D table, field-by-field assignment, then BeginMode3D(camera) around a cube and a grid.

sections.title: Other 3D Calls
paragraphs: Shapes, lines and points in 3D take a table with x, y, z. Note that most 3D draw calls need BeginMode3D first, and that lighting is not part of the binding — the shapes are drawn with flat colors.

code.src:
local origin = { x = 0.0, y = 0.0, z = 0.0 }

raylib.BeginMode3D(camera)
    raylib.DrawSphere({ x = -4.0, y = 1.0, z = 0.0 }, 1.0, raylib.BLUE)
    raylib.DrawCylinder({ x = 0.0, y = 1.0, z = 0.0 }, 0.5, 0.5, 2.0, 16, raylib.GREEN)
    raylib.DrawPlane(origin, { x = 20.0, y = 20.0 }, raylib.LIGHTGRAY)
    raylib.DrawLine3D(origin, { x = 0.0, y = 5.0, z = 0.0 }, raylib.YELLOW)
raylib.EndMode3D()

sections.title: Opening the Device
paragraphs: Audio is started explicitly with InitAudioDevice() and released with CloseAudioDevice(). Between the two, IsAudioDeviceReady() reports whether a device actually opened — worth checking, because a machine without a sound device would otherwise fail later with a confusing error.

rows: Short effect, whole file in memory

sections.title: Sound Effects
paragraphs: LoadSound returns a handle — an integer kept in a variable, exactly like a texture. The same sound may be played again while it is still playing, which is what you want for footsteps or shots.
Trigger it from inside the input check so it fires once per event rather than once per frame.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Sound")
raylib.InitAudioDevice()

if not raylib.IsAudioDeviceReady() then
    print("no audio device available")
end

local beep = raylib.LoadSound("assets/beep.wav")
raylib.SetMasterVolume(0.5)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    if raylib.IsKeyPressed(raylib.KEY_SPACE) then
        raylib.PlaySound(beep)
    end

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.DARKGRAY)
    raylib.DrawText("press space to beep", 40, 90, 20, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.UnloadSound(beep)
raylib.CloseAudioDevice()
raylib.CloseWindow()

sections.title: Music Streams
paragraphs: Music is streamed from disk so a track can be minutes long — but the stream must be fed every frame with UpdateMusicStream(m). Forget that call and the music plays for a fraction of a second and stops.
Put it at the top of the loop, next to the input checks.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(400, 200, "Music")
raylib.InitAudioDevice()

local music = raylib.LoadMusicStream("assets/theme.ogg")
raylib.PlayMusicStream(music)
raylib.SetMusicVolume(music, 0.6)

local paused = false

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    raylib.UpdateMusicStream(music)     -- must run every frame

    if raylib.IsKeyPressed(raylib.KEY_SPACE) then
        if paused then raylib.ResumeMusicStream(music)
        else raylib.PauseMusicStream(music) end
        paused = not paused
    end

    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.BLACK)
    raylib.DrawText(paused and "paused" or "playing", 150, 90, 24, raylib.RAYWHITE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseAudioDevice()
raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: Every loaded sound and music stream is GPU/CPU memory. Free them with UnloadSound / UnloadMusicStream when the game ends.

sections.title: The Rectangle Comes First
paragraphs: The Lua raygui binding is rect-first: a widget takes a raylib.Rectangle as its first argument and the label after it. This differs from the GCL binding, where the rectangle is set beforehand with Raylib.Rectangle(...) and the widget is then called with the text alone.
Widgets return their new state: a button returns a boolean, a slider returns a number.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(600, 400, "raygui")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

local buttonRect = raylib.Rectangle(20, 20, 200, 40)
local sliderRect = raylib.Rectangle(20, 80, 300, 30)
local width = 200.0

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RAYWHITE)

    if raygui.GuiButton(buttonRect, "Reset") then
        width = 200.0
    end

    width = raygui.GuiSlider(sliderRect, "", "Width", width, 50.0, 500.0)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(20, 140, width, 60, raylib.SKYBLUE)
    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: GuiButton returns a Lua boolean, so if raygui.GuiButton(...) reads naturally — no == 1 comparison as in GCL.

sections.title: The Widgets
paragraphs: All of these take a Rectangle first. The ones listed with a return value hand back the new state after the user interacted with them.
Build each Rectangle once, outside the loop, and reuse it — the userdata keeps its fields until you change them.

sections.title: A Settings Panel
paragraphs: Widgets are plain calls, so a panel is just a sequence of them. Note how the value has to be written back: GuiSlider returns the slider's new value, and the slider itself keeps no state of its own.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(480, 300, "Settings")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)

local volume = 0.7
local fullscreen = false
local difficulty = 1

local panelRect = raylib.Rectangle(20, 20, 440, 260)
local volRect   = raylib.Rectangle(40, 80, 380, 30)
local checkRect = raylib.Rectangle(40, 140, 24, 24)
local diffRect  = raylib.Rectangle(40, 190, 200, 30)
local closeRect = raylib.Rectangle(160, 240, 160, 36)

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.DARKGRAY)

    raygui.GuiPanel(panelRect, "Settings")

    volume = raygui.GuiSlider(volRect, "Vol", "", volume, 0.0, 1.0)
    raylib.SetMasterVolume(volume)

    fullscreen = raygui.GuiCheckBox(checkRect, "Fullscreen", fullscreen)

    difficulty = raygui.GuiComboBox(diffRect, "Easy;Normal;Hard", difficulty)

    if raygui.GuiButton(closeRect, "Close") then
        break
    end

    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: The combo box text is one string with semicolon-separated entries: "Easy;Normal;Hard". GuiComboBox returns the selected index.

sections.title: What We Are Building
paragraphs: One window, one paddle, one ball, a score, a click on every hit and a restart button. It uses every part of this track: tables for state, functions for update and draw, input, audio, and a raygui button.
The shape of the file is the shape of every game you will write: constants → state → update → draw → loop.

code.src:
raylib.InitWindow(800, 600, "Keep-Up")
raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)
raylib.InitAudioDevice()
gcl.init()

local WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 600
local PADDLE_W, PADDLE_H = 120, 16
local BALL_R = 8
local PADDLE_SPEED = 420.0
local BALL_SPEED_X = 200.0
local BALL_SPEED_Y = 260.0

local state = {
    paddle_x = WIDTH / 2 - PADDLE_W / 2,
    ball_x = WIDTH / 2,
    ball_y = HEIGHT / 2,
    ball_vx = BALL_SPEED_X,
    ball_vy = -BALL_SPEED_Y,
    score = 0,
    game_over = false,
}

local beep = raylib.LoadSound("assets/beep.wav")
local restart = raylib.Rectangle(WIDTH / 2 - 100, HEIGHT / 2 + 40, 200, 44)

local function reset_ball()
    state.ball_x = WIDTH / 2
    state.ball_y = HEIGHT / 2
    state.ball_vx = state.ball_vx >= 0 and BALL_SPEED_X or -BALL_SPEED_X
    state.ball_vy = -BALL_SPEED_Y
end

local function update(dt)
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_LEFT) then
        state.paddle_x = state.paddle_x - PADDLE_SPEED * dt
    end
    if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_RIGHT) then
        state.paddle_x = state.paddle_x + PADDLE_SPEED * dt
    end
    state.paddle_x = math.max(0, math.min(WIDTH - PADDLE_W, state.paddle_x))

    if state.game_over then return end

    state.ball_x = state.ball_x + state.ball_vx * dt
    state.ball_y = state.ball_y + state.ball_vy * dt

    if state.ball_x - BALL_R <= 0 and state.ball_vx < 0 then
        state.ball_x = BALL_R
        state.ball_vx = -state.ball_vx
    end
    if state.ball_x + BALL_R >= WIDTH and state.ball_vx > 0 then
        state.ball_x = WIDTH - BALL_R
        state.ball_vx = -state.ball_vx
    end
    if state.ball_y - BALL_R <= 0 and state.ball_vy < 0 then
        state.ball_y = BALL_R
        state.ball_vy = -state.ball_vy
    end

    if state.ball_y + BALL_R >= HEIGHT - PADDLE_H and state.ball_vy > 0 then
        if state.ball_x >= state.paddle_x and state.ball_x <= state.paddle_x + PADDLE_W then
            state.ball_y = HEIGHT - PADDLE_H - BALL_R
            state.ball_vy = -state.ball_vy
            state.score = state.score + 1
            raylib.PlaySound(beep)
        else
            state.game_over = true
            gcl.set_state("score", state.score)
        end
    end
end

local function draw()
    raylib.BeginDrawing()
    raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.BLACK)

    raylib.DrawRectangle(state.paddle_x, HEIGHT - PADDLE_H, PADDLE_W, PADDLE_H, raylib.SKYBLUE)
    raylib.DrawCircle(state.ball_x, state.ball_y, BALL_R, raylib.RED)
    raylib.DrawText("score " .. state.score, 20, 20, 30, raylib.RAYWHITE)

    if state.game_over then
        raylib.DrawText("game over", WIDTH / 2 - 80, HEIGHT / 2 - 40, 30, raylib.RAYWHITE)
        if raygui.GuiButton(restart, "Restart") then
            state.score = 0
            state.game_over = false
            reset_ball()
        end
    end

    raylib.EndDrawing()
end

while not raylib.WindowShouldClose() do
    local dt = raylib.GetFrameTime()
    update(dt)
    draw()
end

raylib.UnloadSound(beep)
raylib.CloseAudioDevice()
raylib.CloseWindow()

notes.text: The file runs unchanged whether you launch it with gcl -luarun keepup.lua or let a GCL program start it through Embed.Run(type="lua").

sections.title: Where the Pieces Came From
paragraphs: Nothing in this file is new. Each line is a chapter from this track, and recognising that is the point of the project.

sections.title: Sharing the Score With GCL
paragraphs: The one line worth its own note is gcl.set_state("score", state.score). It publishes the final score into the shared state block, where the GCL program that started this script can read it back with Embed.GetValue(type="lua", name="score") after Embed.Stop(type="lua") returns.
That is the whole cross-language contract: names, numbers, and a call on each side.
